cust_synth_017:C11.body:
Customer Andre Haddad came into the branch today around 2:30 PM. He's a local, lives over in Atlanta, GA, and was pleasant to work with. He had his Chase Slate Edge card (*7093) ready for identification. I greeted him and brought him back to my desk. Standard verification procedures followed.

ID SCAN COMPLETE - GA DL / CUST VERIFIED VIA PIN PAD

Mr. Haddad said he needed to get a cashier's check. He's working on a project, he said, and needed to pay a specialist vendor. When I asked for the amount and the payee name, he got a little flustered. He had the amount ready but had to check his phone for the exact spelling of the business name. He laughed and said his memory wasn't what it used to be. While he was looking, I made some small talk. I noticed the notes on his file and mentioned I was glad to see that issue with the florist had been resolved in his favor. He nodded and said, "Oh, yeah, the $602.64 thing. What a headache that was." He seemed genuinely relieved it was over and appreciative that I'd noticed. He said dealing with dispute DSP-2174159 had been a pain but the resolution was handled well once it got going.

He found the payee name on his phone ("Vintage Steel Restorations LLC") and I began the process of drawing up the check from his primary checking. As the system was loading, he suddenly switched topics completely.

He leaned forward a bit and lowered his voice, "You know, while I'm here, I have a kind of general question. Not something I'm doing today, or even soon, but I was just thinking about it. What's the process if someone wants to close their accounts?" He immediately put his hands up, very insistent, and said, "I am NOT closing the account, I just want to know what the steps would be. I've been with you guys for years, I'm just curious about the procedure."

I assured him it was a perfectly normal question and that I was happy to walk him through the hypothetical steps. I explained that he could do it in a branch, over the phone, or by written request. We'd need to make sure all his balances were zero and that there were no pending transactions. I mentioned that for his credit card, any remaining rewards points would be forfeited upon closure, so it's always best to redeem them beforehand. I also mentioned that closing a long-held credit card can sometimes have a small impact on a person's credit score due to the change in average age of accounts and credit utilization, so it's something to be aware of.

He seemed to be listening intently. He asked a few follow-up questions about whether it was instant or took a few days. I explained that once initiated, it's pretty quick, but we always advise waiting a few business days after the last transaction clears just to be safe. Since he seemed concerned about the "value" of the account, I took the opportunity to softly pivot to retention. I told him we value his business and that there are often promotions available to long-time customers. I mentioned, just as an example, that we sometimes run targeted offers like a $200.00 statement credit for meeting a certain spend threshold over a few months, and that it's always worth calling the number on the back of his card to see if any offers are available to him. He just nodded and said "good to know," but didn't seem interested in pursuing it, which was fine. His focus was clearly on the "what if" scenario.

While we were on the topic of his account, I also confirmed his contact information was up to date. I said, "I see we have your email as haddad.a65@example.net and the best call-back number as 502-555-0157, is that all still correct?" He confirmed it was. He mentioned the new phone number was his work landline and it was much more reliable for callbacks. I also saw the note about his canceled trip and said something like, "I was sorry to see your trip to Mexico City had to be postponed, hopefully you get to reschedule it soon." He waved his hand and said, "That's life. The car restoration is my vacation now."

Then, as if a switch flipped, he went right back to the original topic. "Okay, so, the check. Sorry for the detour. Are we all set on that?" I confirmed I had everything I needed and just required his signature on the withdrawal slip and the cashier's check log. I printed the check, he verified the spelling of the payee and the amount one last time, and I handed it to him in a bank envelope with the carbon copy receipt. He thanked me for my patience and for answering his "weird questions." He said he was heading straight to the auto shop to drop off the deposit. Seemed excited. Overall a very positive interaction despite the slightly unusual line of questioning.

Follow-up:
Customer inquired about account closure process but was adamant he is not planning to close. May be a sign of future attrition risk or could just be simple curiosity. No action needed at this time, but recommend flagging account for proactive retention offers in Q4 if spending on *7093 slows or if balances begin to be drawn down significantly. Continue to use 502-555-0157 for any outbound contact.

IVR: Thank you. For security, please say or enter the four-digit year of your birth.

IVR: Thank you. Please listen carefully as our menu options have recently changed. For account balance and activity, say "Balance." For payments, say "Payments." For rewards, say "Rewards." To report a card lost or stolen, say "Lost card." For all other inquiries, or to speak with a representative, say "Agent."

CUSTOMER: Agent.

IVR: Connecting you to the next available agent. Wait times are currently between three and five minutes.

(Music on hold)

AGENT: Thank you for holding, my name is Brenda, how can I help you today?

AGENT: I can certainly help you with that. To make sure I'm speaking with the account holder, could you please confirm your full name and your home city and state for me?

CUSTOMER: Andre Haddad. Atlanta, Georgia.

AGENT: Thank you, Mr. Haddad. I have your account pulled up here. Just one moment while I review the notes... Okay, I see the dispute you're referring to. For chargebacks and disputes, I'll need to transfer you over to our specialized department. They'll have the most up-to-date information for you. Is that okay?

CUSTOMER: Yes, that's fine. As long as I don't get disconnected. The last time I called you guys the call dropped right in the middle of activating my new card.

AGENT: Oh, I'm very sorry to hear that, sir. I see the notes on that call from last month. I'll make sure this is a warm transfer, so you won't have to explain everything again. Please hold.

(Music on hold)

HOLD MESSAGE: Did you know you can manage your account twenty-four-seven online at chase.com? Check your balance, make a payment, and even redeem your Ultimate Rewards points. It's fast, easy, and secure. Thank you for your patience. An agent will be with you shortly.

(Click)

AGENT: Hello Mr. Haddad, my name is Tom. I'm a specialist in the disputes department. I understand you're calling about a chargeback?

CUSTOMER: Yes, finally. Hello, Tom.

AGENT: Hello, sir. So, my colleague Brenda tells me you're calling about a dispute regarding a charge for some... uh, was it furniture? For around six hundred dollars?

CUSTOMER: No, not furniture. It was flowers. For a wedding. From a place called Harbor Lights Florist. The amount was $602.64. They delivered the wrong flowers, half of them were dead... it was a complete disaster.

AGENT: Oh, I see. My apologies, I must have misread the note. Flowers, not furniture. I'm very sorry to hear about that experience, that sounds incredibly stressful. Let me get the case file pulled up for you. Okay... I'm looking at dispute DSP-2174159. The charge date was back in May for $602.64. Is that the one?

CUSTOMER: That's the one. I sent in photos, I sent in emails, I did everything I was told to do. And then... nothing. Silence.

AGENT: I understand your frustration, sir, and I appreciate your patience. Let's see what's going on here. I'm reviewing the timeline now. Okay... okay. Well, Mr. Haddad, I actually have some good news for you.

CUSTOMER: I could use some.

AGENT: It looks like we concluded our investigation last week. We gave the merchant, Harbor Lights Florist, the standard forty-five days to respond to the dispute and provide evidence to support the charge. According to our records, they never responded.

CUSTOMER: So? What does that mean?

AGENT: It means the case is closed, and it's been decided in your favor. The temporary credit of $602.64 that was applied to your account is now permanent.

CUSTOMER: Permanent? So it's... it's over? They can't recharge me?

AGENT: That is correct. The credit is permanent. The matter is officially closed.

CUSTOMER: Oh, thank God. You have no idea. My wife has been asking me about this every single day. It's just... it's been a nightmare. Getting this new card was a hassle, then this... it's been one thing after another.

AGENT: I can only imagine. Well, I'm glad I could give you the good news today. It's all settled.

AGENT: Can you please confirm the home city you have on file with us?

CUSTOMER: Oh yeah, finally got around to that. It's haddad dot a six five at example dot net.
AGENT: Excellent, thank you for verifying that for me. I have your account pulled up. So how can I help you, Mr. Haddad?
CUSTOMER: Okay, so, two things really. First, I was, uh, I was in a branch a couple weeks ago, must have been the end of August, getting a cashier's check. I wanted to see if I was eligible for that, or how it works. I'm not seeing anything about it on my account online.
AGENT: Okay, I can certainly look into that promotion for you. You said you heard about it at a branch visit?
CUSTOMER: Yeah, that's right. I was just in there asking some general questions about the account, you know, what if this what if that, and he brought it up.
AGENT: I understand. Some of our offers are targeted, so they might not appear for everyone online. Do you mind if I place you on a brief hold while I check the notes on your account and look up the details for that specific offer? It shouldn't take more than two to three minutes.

AGENT: Thank you, I'll be right back.

AGENT: Thank you for holding, Mr. Haddad.
CUSTOMER: Yep. Back.
AGENT: Okay, so I am seeing the notes from your branch visit at the end of last month. And I do see the promotion you're referring to. It's an offer for a $200.00 statement credit. CUSTOMER: See, that's what I thought. It sounded like a new-customer thing, but he made it sound like, you know, it was for existing customers too. Look, it's not like I'm trying to get a free flight to Paris tomorrow, I just want to understand the offer. I've had this card for years.
AGENT: I completely understand, sir. The marketing materials can sometimes be general. Let me just read the fine print here for you... Hmm. Okay, it looks like there *is* a version of it for existing cardholders, but it's what we call a targeted digital offer. AGENT: Right, I do see the thread here from mid-August. It looks like that was all taken care of and the haddad.a65 email is the primary one on file now.
CUSTOMER: Yeah, but I never got an email about a promo. Not to the new one, not to the old one. So I guess I don't qualify? Is that it?
AGENT: It does seem like your account wasn't targeted for this specific campaign, sir. I'm sorry about that. The information you received at the branch may have been more general in nature.
CUSTOMER: Huh. Okay. Well, that's annoying. [inaudible] the way he said it... Okay, fine. Forget that for a second. Can I ask something else while I have you on the line?
AGENT: Of course, what is it?
CUSTOMER: What's my statement closing date for this month? For September.
AGENT: Yes, I can get that for you. One moment while I pull up your cycle dates.
CUSTOMER: I'm just trying to time a purchase, you know, and I want to make sure it falls on the next statement, not the current one that's about to be due pretty soon.
AGENT: I understand completely. A lot of people do that. Okay, so looking at your billing cycle, your next statement will close on... September 25th.
CUSTOMER: The twenty-fifth. Okay. So any purchase I make before the twenty-fifth will be on the bill that's due in October, and anything on the twenty-sixth would be on the one for November. Is that right?
AGENT: That's... almost right. Anything you purchase up to and including September 25th will appear on your September statement, which will then have a due date in October. AGENT: You're very welcome. Was there anything else?
CUSTOMER: Actually, yeah, let's go back to the rewards thing. So there's really no way to get that two hundred dollar credit.
AGENT: I'm not seeing a way to manually add that specific offer to your account since it was a targeted campaign you weren't enrolled in, I do apologize. I've checked all the available options for that particular campaign.

It's all in the rewards portal online.
CUSTOMER: Hmm. So there's no, like... bonus offer or anything I *do* qualify for? I've been a customer for a long time, always pay on time. You guys were great, actually, helping me out with that dispute a couple months ago... for that, uh, what was it, Harbor Lights Florence? CUSTOMER: Yeah, that was great. So you see, I'm a good customer! [chuckles] Isn't there anything you can do? Any little bonus? Twenty bucks? Anything? It was a little misleading at the branch.
AGENT: [chuckles] I appreciate you asking, Mr. Haddad, and we do value your loyalty. Let me just take another look here at the offers tab specifically for your account... I'm not one to give up easily. One moment please.
CUSTOMER: Thanks, Anjali. I appreciate it.
AGENT: Okay... hm. It's not a statement credit, but I do see an offer you can activate right now. It's for bonus points at grocery stores and for spending on streaming services for the next three months. It's 5% back in those categories.
CUSTOMER: Oh. Grocery stores. Huh. And streaming. That's actually... that's actually pretty good. My wife and I spend a lot on groceries. How do I... do you do it? Or do I have to go online?
AGENT: I can activate it for you right now, if you'd like. The bonus earning would start today.
CUSTOMER: Yes. Yes, please, that would be great. Activate it.
AGENT: Okay, just a moment. I am adding the offer to your Slate Edge card now... and... there. It's all set. You'll now earn 5% back on purchases in those categories for the next 90 days, up to a certain spending limit which you'll be able to see in the confirmation email.
AGENT: Okay, that makes sense.
CUSTOMER: Great. So an email will come through? To the haddad dot a six five address?
AGENT: Yes, that's correct. It should arrive within 24 hours. So, just to recap our call, I've activated the 5% bonus points offer for you on groceries and streaming, and we confirmed your statement closing date is the 25th of the month. Did you have any other questions for me today?
CUSTOMER: No, I think that's everything. You know, I'm still a little bummed about the two hundred dollars, but this bonus point thing is something, so... thank you for finding that.
AGENT: You are most welcome. I'm happy I could find something for you. Is there anything else at all?
CUSTOMER: Nope, that's it for me. I'm good.
AGENT: Alright. Well, thank you for calling Chase, Mr. Haddad. For your records, the case number for this call is CASE-3841146. Have a wonderful rest of your day.
CUSTOMER: You too, Anjali. Thanks again. Bye.
AGENT: Goodbye.

IVR: Thank you for calling Chase Card Services. Your call may be monitored or recorded for quality assurance.
IVR: To continue in English, press one. Para continuar en español, oprima dos.
(keypad tone)
IVR: Please say or enter your full sixteen-digit card number.
(keypad tones)
IVR: Thank you. For security, please enter your date of birth, as two digits for the month, two for the day, and four for the year.
(keypad tones)
IVR: Thank you. Please listen carefully as our menu options have recently changed. For account balance and activity, press one. To make a payment, press two. To report your card lost or stolen, press three. For questions about a dispute, or to file a new dispute, press four. For all other inquiries, press zero, or stay on the line.
(keypad tone)
IVR: You have selected questions about a dispute. Please hold while I transfer you to the next available agent.

HOLD MESSAGE: Did you know you can manage your account twenty-four-seven online at chase.com or with the Chase Mobile app? Check your balance, pay your bill, and even lock your card with the touch of a button. Stay on the line, an agent will be with you shortly. Your current wait time is approximately two minutes.

(music on hold for 90 seconds)

AGENT: Thank you for holding, my name is Maria. I’ll be helping you today. I see you’re calling about a dispute. Before we get started, I just need to complete the security verification. Can you please confirm the full name on the account?

CUSTOMER: Yes, it’s Sofia Doyle.

AGENT: Thank you, Ms. Doyle. And can you confirm the billing address, including the zip code?

CUSTOMER: It’s in Charlotte, North Carolina. 1820... um... Willow Creek Lane. Zip is 28202.

AGENT: Perfect, thank you. One moment. Okay, I have your account pulled up here. I see the Chase Slate Edge card ending in **** 2837. How can I help you with a dispute today?

CUSTOMER: Hi. I’m calling because I filed a dispute, oh, about a month ago, I think? And I was just checking my account online and I saw a credit was posted. I just want to know if that means it’s all done, if the case is closed.

AGENT: I can certainly check on that for you. Do you happen to have the dispute number?

CUSTOMER: Oh, lord. Um, I know I got an email. Let me see if I can find it. It was for a charge of... four hundred seventy-three dollars and thirty-one cents.

AGENT: Okay, for $473.31. Let me see... yes, I see a dispute here, DSP-1512689. Is that the one?

CUSTOMER: Yes! That’s it. So, I saw the credit for that amount posted, I think the day before yesterday? And I was hoping that was the end of it.

AGENT: I understand. Yes, I see that a provisional credit for the full amount of $473.31 was posted to your account. That’s a temporary credit we provide while the investigation is still open.

CUSTOMER: Oh. So it’s not… it’s not final? I don’t understand. Does that mean the charge could come back?

AGENT: It simply means the investigation is still in progress, Ms. Doyle. The merchant has a certain amount of time to respond to the dispute with their evidence. The provisional credit is our way of making sure you’re not responsible for the payment while we work through that process.

CUSTOMER: Right, but what is that process? How long does it take? The last person I talked to was very vague about it. It’s been over a month already.

AGENT: The standard timeframe can be up to two billing cycles, but it often resolves much faster. I don’t have a specific end date here in my system, I’m afraid. The investigation is being handled by our back-office disputes team.

CUSTOMER: Is there someone there I can talk to? I just feel like I'm in the dark here. I get an email, then nothing, then a credit just shows up with no explanation. I’d really like to speak with someone who can tell me what’s actually happening. A supervisor, maybe?

AGENT: I understand your frustration, Ms. Doyle. I can’t transfer you directly to a back-office supervisor, but I can transfer you to a senior account specialist who has more visibility into the dispute process. Would you like me to do that?

CUSTOMER: Yes, please. If they can give me a real answer, that would be great.

AGENT: Of course. Please hold one moment while I transfer you.

(click)

HOLD MESSAGE: Your financial health is our priority. Explore tools like Credit Journey, free for all Chase customers, to monitor your credit score without impacting it. An agent will be with you shortly.

(music on hold for 60 seconds)

AGENT: Thank you for holding, this is Rafael. I’m a senior account specialist. I understand you’re calling about an open dispute?

CUSTOMER: Yes, finally. My name is Sofia Doyle. I was just talking to someone else.

AGENT: Yes, I have the notes here from Maria. Just to confirm for my own records, you are the primary account holder, Sofia Doyle?

CUSTOMER: I am.

AGENT: Thank you. So, let me just recap. I see you’re calling about dispute DSP-1512689, regarding a charge from Kohl’s for $473.31. You saw the provisional credit and wanted to know if the case was closed. Is that correct?

CUSTOMER: No, that’s not right. Not entirely. I mean, the amount is right, but the charge wasn’t from Kohl’s. I think I might have mentioned that name on the first call, when I was just guessing, but the charge was from a company called Golden Gate Luggage Co. That’s what’s on the statement.

AGENT: Ah, my apologies. Thank you for the correction. I see that noted further down in the original case file. Golden Gate Luggage Co. Let me pull up the full details on that dispute for you. Just one moment.

(typing sounds)

AGENT: Okay. Yes, Ms. Doyle, I have everything here. Dispute DSP-1512689 was opened on March fourth regarding that charge. And I do see that the provisional credit for $473.31 was applied to your account. That posted the day before yesterday.

CUSTOMER: Right. So what does that mean? The last agent said it’s not final.

AGENT: That is correct. "Provisional" just means it’s temporary. We’ve given you the money back while we complete our investigation. At this point, we have sent the details to the merchant’s bank, and we are waiting for them to respond. They can either accept the dispute, in which case the credit becomes permanent and the case is closed, or they can provide evidence that the charge is valid.

CUSTOMER: And if they do that? Then what?

AGENT: If they provide evidence—like a receipt with your signature, or shipping confirmation to your address—we would review it. If the evidence seems valid, we would have to reverse the provisional credit, and the charge would reappear on your statement. But you would be notified before that happens, and you’d have an opportunity to rebut their evidence.

CUSTOMER: This is so complicated. I just want to know when it will be over. Can’t you give me a date?

AGENT: I can’t give you an exact date, I’m sorry. It really depends on how and when the merchant responds. While I’m reviewing the file here... I can see a note from a few weeks ago. And Ms. Doyle, just as a note on your account, I see the request for a credit line increase was declined last month. The system shows you can request that again after October 10, 2026, and if you keep the requested amount under $4,000.00, it generally avoids the manual underwriting process which can speed things up.

CUSTOMER: Oh. Okay, I'm not really worried about that right now. I just want to solve this dispute. It’s for a lot of money. Can you at least tell me if the merchant has even looked at it yet? Is there any activity?

AGENT: Let me see... It doesn’t appear that a response has been received yet. That’s not unusual. They have a set period to work with. Hold on, my wife is asking me something. One second.
RENATA: (muffled in background) Ask him if he needs my number.
CUSTOMER: (to Renata) He can’t talk to you. (to agent) Sorry about that. My wife is also concerned about this.

RENATA: (now closer to the phone) Hi, sorry, is this about the luggage charge? I just wanted to make sure they have my number too in case they need to call. It's 608-555-0619. I'm an authorized user, but on my own card, the one ending in 4393, but this charge was on Sofia's card. We just want it sorted.

AGENT: I appreciate that, ma'am, and I understand your concern. However, for security and privacy reasons, I can only discuss account specifics with the primary account holder, Ms. Doyle. And any callbacks from us would need to go to a number we verify directly with her.

CUSTOMER: It’s fine, Renata. Let me handle it. (to agent) Sorry about that, Rafael. She’s just anxious. So, you can’t tell me anything more about the timeline? This is really frustrating. I want to talk to a supervisor. Someone who can actually do something.

AGENT: I do understand. A supervisor would have access to the same information that I have, Ms. Doyle. They also cannot force the merchant to respond faster. But what I can do is document your request for an update and a clearer timeline. I can open a new case file for this specific call and your request, and I can have a supervisor from the dispute resolution team review it.

CUSTOMER: And then what? They’ll email me another form letter?

AGENT: No, I can request that they call you directly. Do you have a good callback number where they can reach you during business hours?

CUSTOMER: Yes. Yes, that would be better. Use my office landline. It’s 608-555-0488… no, wait, that’s the old fax line, sorry. Hang on. It’s 608-555-0481.

AGENT: Okay, thank you. Let me read that back. The best number to reach you is 608-555-0481.

CUSTOMER: Yes, that’s the one. 0-4-8-1 at the end.

AGENT: Got it. I am opening a new case for you now, the reference number for this interaction is CASE-1460630. I've noted down all your concerns and your request for a status update. I am putting in a request right now for a supervisor to call back on that number, the 608-555-0481. You should hear from them by Friday at the latest.

CUSTOMER: By this coming Friday?

AGENT: Yes, by Friday. They will review the current status of dispute DSP-1512689 and call you with any updates they have.

CUSTOMER: Okay. I guess that’s something. A real person calling me back would be a big improvement. Make sure they have that case number, the… DSP one.

AGENT: They will have all of this information, Ms. Doyle. I’ve linked this new case, CASE-1460630, directly to the dispute file. The supervisor will have the full history.

CUSTOMER: Okay. Thank you, Rafael.

AGENT: You’re very welcome. I’m sorry again for the frustrating process. Is there anything else I can assist you with today?

CUSTOMER: No, that’s it. I’ll just wait for the call.

AGENT: Sounds good. Thank you for calling Chase, Ms. Doyle, and have a good rest of your day.

CUSTOMER: You too. Bye.

(call ends)
